blocks.text: The ¹³C NMR spectrum is simpler than ¹H NMR in which each peak (or signal) corresponds to a single, different environment or type of carbon atom. Chemical shift of each peak tells about its environment.

blocks.latex: \text{The number of peaks} = \text{The number of different carbon environments}
blocks.text_alt: The number of peaks = The number of different carbon environments

blocks.text: ¹³C NMR spectrum of ethane shows only one peak as both the carbon atoms have the same environment. In propane CH₃ – CH₂ – CH₃, there are two types of carbon environments, the two terminal -CH₃ carbons have the same environment while the middle -CH₂- carbon has a different environment. The ¹³C NMR spectrum of propane shows two peaks, one for the methyl carbon atoms while the other for -CH₂- carbon atom. Similarly, two peaks are observed in the ¹³C spectrum of ethanol (CH₃–CH₂–OH), due to the presence of two types of environments in this molecule (Figure 30.7).

blocks.alt: On a pale yellow panel, a 13C NMR spectrum on a ppm scale from 60 to 0: a green line near 57 ppm, a pink line near 18 ppm and a line labelled TMS at 0. Inset: the displayed formula HO-C-C-H of ethanol with the carbon next to OH in green and the other carbon in pink.
blocks.caption: Figure 30.7: 13C NMR spectrum of ethanol (original drawing after the textbook's figure).

blocks.text: Analyzing the ¹³C NMR spectrum of ethanol by using the data given in Table 30.3, it is evident that the peak at 18 ppm is for -CH₃ carbon, while the peak near 57 ppm is due to -CH₂- carbon atom.

There are two key differences between ¹H NMR and ¹³C NMR spectra. The relative peak area in ¹³C NMR is usually not proportional to the number of carbon atoms unlike ¹H NMR in which peak area shows the number of protons. Secondly, the peaks do not show splitting, hence these appear as vertical lines. Due to this, ¹³C NMR technique is less sensitive than ¹H NMR.
book_errors: Due to this, ¹³C NMR technique is less sensitive than ¹H NMR.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The lack of splitting is not the reason. ¹³C NMR is less sensitive than ¹H NMR because only about 1.1% of carbon atoms are ¹³C and the ¹³C nucleus gives a much weaker signal, so many scans are needed.

blocks.prompt: a) How many signals do you expect to observe in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of butane? Justify your answer.
blocks.explanation: Two: CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ is the same from both ends, so the two CH₃ carbons are equivalent and the two CH₂ carbons are equivalent.

blocks.prompt: b) Predict the ¹³C NMR spectrum of butan-2-ol.
blocks.explanation: Four peaks, one for each carbon of CH₃–CH(OH)–CH₂–CH₃: the C–O carbon at 50 – 70 ppm (about 69) and three alkyl carbons at 0 – 50 ppm (about 32, 23 and 10).

blocks.prompt: c) Predict the chemical shift of carbon atoms in propanoic acid.
blocks.explanation: Three peaks for CH₃CH₂COOH: the COOH carbon at 160 – 185 ppm; the CH₂ next to the carboxyl group in the 30 – 65 ppm range of Table 30.3 (actually about 28 ppm); the CH₃ at 0 – 50 ppm (about 9 ppm).
